message.content:
**Triangulation metrics** are quantitative measures that describe the characteristics, quality, and performance of a triangulation—whether it’s a geometric mesh, a network graph, or a computational run that produces a set of triangles. In practice they fall into two broad categories: | Category | Typical metrics | What they tell you | |----------|-----------------|--------------------| | **Mesh‑quality / Geometry** | • **Number of triangles**
• **Average/median triangle area**
• **Minimum/maximum edge length**
• **Aspect ratio** (ratio of longest to shortest side)
• **Minimum/maximum internal angle**
• **Skewness / distortion** | How fine or coarse the mesh is, how uniform the triangles are, and whether any triangles are “bad” (e.g., skinny or highly distorted). | | **Algorithmic / Performance** | • **Runtime** (seconds/minutes)
• **Memory usage** (bytes/MB)
• **Number of iterations / passes**
• **Convergence tolerance achieved**
• **Number of re‑triangulations / refinements** | How efficiently the triangulation algorithm ran, how many resources it consumed, and whether it met its convergence or quality targets. | ### Why they matter 1. **Quality Assurance** – In engineering, GIS, or computer graphics, a high‑quality mesh ensures accurate simulations, rendering, or spatial analyses. Metrics help flag problematic triangles early. 2. **Performance Tuning** – Knowing runtime and memory consumption lets developers optimize code or choose better hardware. 3. **Comparability** – When comparing different products or branches (as in your API call), triangulation metrics give a common yardstick to evaluate which implementation performs better or produces higher‑quality meshes. ### Example Use‑Case Suppose you have two branches of a software product that both generate terrain meshes from satellite data. By pulling the latest 90‑day triangulation runs via the API, you can extract metrics such as: - Branch A produced 1 200 000 triangles with an average area of 0.45 m², runtime 12 s, memory 350 MB. - Branch B produced 1 250 000 triangles with an average area of 0.42 m², runtime 15 s, memory 400 MB. From this you can conclude that Branch B yields slightly finer meshes but at a higher computational cost. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics quantify *how* a triangulation looks (geometry) and *how* it was produced (performance). They’re essential for debugging, optimization, and ensuring that the output meets the required standards.
